lines: Jordan Lee
+1 (555) 010-2468 | jordan.lee@example.com | example.com/code/jordan-lee
EDUCATION
Western State University | M.S. in Computer Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2024 - Expected Jun 2026
Eastern Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, Country | Sep 2018 - Jun 2022
EXPERIENCE
Eastern Robotics Co. | Junior Software Engineer | Metro City, Country | Aug 2022 - Jul 2024
- Owned the diagnostics service's monitoring dashboards across two major releases and the on-call rotation that used them.
- Reduced p95 API latency from 420 ms to 180 ms by adding a request cache and batching sensor reads, with load tests that fail the build if p95 exceeds 200 ms.
- Maintained the CI pipeline for the perception team's model releases, adding automated regression checks that shortened release cycles from 2 weeks to 3 days.

- Migrated 30 robot-fleet services from cron jobs to an event queue while rewriting the shared logging library, onboarding two new hires and taking over the weekend on-call rotation, which removed the nightly backlogs that delayed morning dispatch.
Mobility Systems Company | Machine Learning Engineering Intern | Metro City, USA | Oct 2024 - May 2025

- Built a diagnostics triage branch for an industrial inspection system that screens 800+ sensor signals per case with ML-extracted features, cutting the pending-case backlog 68% in the eight weeks after launch.
- Raised diagnostic accuracy on 1,200 held-out cases from 71% to 79% by fine-tuning a domain adapter on validated tool-use trajectories with assistant-only loss masking.
- Cut p95 latency of single-request edge inference by 40% by serving the INT8 engine with dynamic batching.
- Using grouped tool-use rollouts, a composite reward over accuracy, citation validity and call count, and a GRPO loop with a frozen SFT reference, reduced end-to-end latency 5%.
- Stabilised GRPO training on sparse rewards by sampling a single rollout per prompt, so each update used exactly one scored trajectory.
- Documented the triage branch's abstention rules and escalation paths for the on-call reviewers, who adopted them as the team's runbook.
PROJECTS
Agent Runtime Suite | Owner | TypeScript, Multi-Agent Systems | Aug 2025 - Present
- Drove adoption of AI-first engineering practices across the platform, accelerating delivery and improving outcomes for downstream teams.
- Cut p95 tool-call latency from 900 ms to 600 ms, a 50% reduction, by caching tool results and reusing completed sub-agent answers.
- Raised the runtime's task-completion rate by 12% on the benchmark suite, from 71% to 83%, by retrying failed sub-agent calls with their partial context.
Research-Agent Evaluation Framework | Contributor | LLM Evaluation | Feb 2025 - Jul 2025
- Upstreamed 8 citation and faithfulness metrics to an open-source research-agent framework, where they now run in the default benchmark for every release.
- Showed the evaluator tracks injected degradation with a Kendall correlation of 0.89 across 400+ report-level trials that removed citations, sources and claims.
- Traced 3 structural pipeline defects in stability, sourcing and parameter handling to their modules with layered instrumentation; each was fixed upstream.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, TypeScript, Git
ML & Agents: PyTorch, LoRA, GRPO, agent evaluation, Kubernetes

items.says: There is no headline or summary establishing the target professional focus.
items.because: Recruiters must infer the ML, agent, and systems focus from the entries below.

items.says: Consider whether education should precede experience for experienced-role applications.
items.because: The work and project evidence may be more persuasive up front.

items.says: Put experience in reverse chronological order.
items.because: The internship ending in May 2025 appears after the role ending in July 2024.

items.says: Keep date formatting and punctuation consistent across the résumé.
Keep the expected graduation date clear and consistent with the other dates.
Show the dashboards’ scale, what changed, and what improved for their users.
items.because: The bullet signals ownership but does not show its impact.

items.says: Show the operational impact of the on-call responsibility.
items.because: It takes up space without showing what that responsibility achieved.

items.says: Make clear that 200 ms is a test limit, not the achieved latency.
items.because: Readers could confuse the threshold with the reported 180 ms result.

items.says: Clarify how the automated checks led to the shorter release cycle.
items.because: The causal claim would feel better supported.

items.says: Consider a stronger verb than “Maintained” if you made significant changes.
items.because: It may understate your contribution.

items.says: Separate or prioritize the many contributions in this bullet.
items.because: The reader cannot easily identify the main result and your role in it.

items.says: Clarify what the final “which” refers to.
items.because: Its antecedent is unclear.

items.says: Add a measure of the backlog impact if available.
items.because: A measure would make the result stronger.

items.says: Avoid repeating the on-call responsibility from the dashboards bullet.
items.because: The on-call reference overlaps with the first bullet.

items.says: Explain what “branch” means to an outside reader.
Make the connection between the triage system and backlog reduction easier to follow.
Consider adding a defensible backlog baseline or further measurement context.
items.because: It could help establish the result beyond the eight weeks after launch.

items.says: Explain how accuracy was measured and what the held-out cases represent.
items.because: Readers may not know how comparable or meaningful the evaluation is.

items.says: Keep the result understandable to a broader engineering reader despite the loss-masking detail.
items.because: That detail is most readily understood by an ML audience.

items.says: Distinguish this 71% accuracy baseline from the project’s 71% task-completion baseline.
items.because: Readers could mistake the unrelated metrics for the same result.

items.says: Explain the workload and measurement setup for single-request inference with dynamic batching.
items.because: Those terms may seem at odds to readers.

items.says: Make the basis for the 40% latency comparison unambiguous.
Rewrite the opening to make clear who or what produced the result.
items.because: Its current construction obscures attribution.

items.says: Clarify the measurement scope and your specific contribution to the 5% latency improvement.
Consider trimming the methodological detail before the result.
items.because: It takes substantial space for a relatively modest latency change.

items.says: Provide evidence that training became more stable or explain the tradeoff of one scored trajectory per update.
items.because: The bullet says what you did without showing why it mattered.

items.says: Standardize the spelling of “Stabilised” with the résumé’s US spelling.
items.because: It differs from the spelling used elsewhere.

items.says: Show what the runbook helped reviewers do, if measurable.
items.because: Its operational impact is not clear from adoption alone.

items.says: Replace or remove the broad “AI-first practices” bullet.
items.because: It does not say what changed or provide an example or measure of its claimed outcomes.

items.says: The 900 ms to 600 ms change is a 33% reduction, not 50%.
items.because: The incorrect arithmetic undermines confidence in other metrics.

items.says: Clarify the latency measurement setup and whether the workload is representative.
items.because: The absolute numbers do not show how broadly the improvement applies.

items.says: Call the change from 71% to 83% a 12-point change rather than leaving it open to a 12% relative reading.
items.because: The two descriptions mean different things.

items.says: Describe the benchmark enough to make task completion interpretable.
Clarify whether this 71% baseline is unrelated to the internship’s 71% accuracy figure.
items.because: Readers could mistake them for the same result.

items.says: Make your personal contribution to the upstreamed metrics clear.
items.because: “Upstreamed” may describe work shared with others.

items.says: Explain what was correlated and what the 0.89 value indicates.
items.because: Readers need an interpretation of the evaluator’s behavior.

items.says: Add the practical effect of the upstream fixes if available.
items.because: The current bullet establishes the investigation and fixes but not their effect.

items.says: Clarify how the three defects relate to the three named areas.
items.because: The phrasing is hard to parse.

items.says: Expand the skills section with relevant skills already demonstrated in the experience.
items.because: The current list undersells the technical range and makes CI, inference serving, and evaluation hard to find quickly.

items.says: Consider replacing Git with a more distinguishing skill, if accurate.
items.because: Git is a low-distinction item for many engineering roles.

items.says: Keep skills entries consistent in specificity.
items.because: Tools, methods, and broad capabilities are currently mixed together.

items.says: Reconsider placing Kubernetes under “ML & Agents.”
items.because: The heading mixes infrastructure with methods and concepts.
